HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK PRIVILEGE-RESIGNATION OF MR. E. GUSS PORTER
speechtext:
Has the Acting Postmaster General any information to give to the House regarding the settlement of the postal strike, with particular reference to Toronto?
Hon. CHARLES A. STEWART (Argen-teuil, Acting Postmaster General):	I have
no new evidence to submit except to say that to-day we have in the neighbourhood of sixty carriers delivering mail in that city. Of course, I do not want the impression to go abroad that we are anything like covering the city, because ordinarily 450 are engaged in delivering mail. Two of the postal stations are being manned to-day and delivery other than by carrier is improving all the time. A personal letter mailed in the afternoon of the 25th instant was delivered to my family this morning. True, it ought to have been received yesterday, but the report the postmaster gives me is that the matter is improving every minute and in a very short time complete mail delivery, not complete carrier delivery, will be re-established.
As regards the men, I have a communication that would indicate that the only grounds upon which they will return are for all of them to be completely re-established.

speechtext:
I might mention to the
House that it is the intention of the government that we should sit on Tuesday the 1st July. I know a number of members have asked the question.

The House resumed from June 26 consideration in committee on Bill No. 47, to incorporate the United Church of Canada-Mr. Forke -Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 3-Definitions.

Counsel for the promoters of this bill, in fact counsel on both sides, have drawn my attention to a number
United Church of Canada

of clerical errors that have appeared from the changing of the numbers in the bill. I move that the word "section" in line 25 on page 2 of the bill be amended to read "act."

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 4, subsection (b)-Corporations and local union congregations.
I move that the subsection be amended by substituting the word "three" for the word "two" in lines 20 and 22.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 6-Property of congregations.
I move to amend the section by striking out the word "seven" in the first line and substituting the word "eight."

Amendment agreed to.
Section as aimended agreed to.
On section 8-Special property of certain congregations.

I move to amend the
section by substituting in lines 8 and 9, in place of the words "four" and "five", the words "five" and "six".

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 9-Existing trustees continued.

I move to amend the
section by substituting in line 15 the word "six" for the word "five".

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 10-Property of non-concurring congregations.

This section provides that
the vote shall be taken by call of a meeting of the congregation. During the discussion in the Private Bills committee some of us thought that this was not the best method of taking the vote; we considered it would ibe far better to have it taken by ballot. If the meeting -were held on a Stormy night a great many people might be unable to attend. There might be others too who would be unable to be present at the meeting owing to sickness or for any other valid reason; and some again might be out of town. I would suggest :to the hon. member (Mr. Forke) who introduced the bill that he accept an amendment to have the vote taken by

ballot instead of ait a regular meeting of (congregation. I therefore move to amend the section by adding:
Provided always that if any congregation in connection or communion with any of the negotiating churches shall, upon a vote of such congregation to be taken by ballot in accordance with the regulations set out in schedule "D" to this act, decide by a majority of the votes cast not to enter the United church, then and in such case the property real and personal belonging to or held in trust for or to the use of such congregation shall remain unaffected by this act, and provided that any church formed by the non-concurring congregations shall stand in the place of the respective negotiating church in respect of any trusts relating to such property. Any vote of any such congregation taken in accordance with the provisions of any act of any province of Canada respecting the United church passed before the passing of this act shall be deemed to be a valid vote for the purposes of this section.
In the two previous votes taken in 1911 and 1915 in the Presbyterian church the ballot was used; ballots were distributed either by session or otherwise to every member in the congregation whether they were able to attend church or not, or even if they were out of town at the time the vote was taken. This ballot was regularly signed and1 witnessed by someone and was returned either to the clerk of session or to some other authorized person. I think this is a reasonable suggestion and I hope the member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) and the rest of the committee will accept it.
How does the hon. member propose to apply this to those persons whose names are still on the church register as members but who have moved a distance away?

If I remember rightly the
bill provides that members who are in full communion at the time of the passing of the act shall be deemed competent to vote for the purposes of the act. Take the hon. gentleman's own case for example, or mine; this vote might be taken while we were in Ottawa. I do not think it would be fair to require either the hon. gentleman or myself to go back home to attend a meeting in order to vote either to remain in the church or to leave it. I think he will immediately see with me that the suggestion I make is only reasonable; I think the right method is to have ballots distributed to the congregation and returned.

I was thinking more of
those who have changed their places of residence permanently.

I believe it is provided in the bill that any one who has changed his

United Church oj Canada
residence may still vote. Probably the hon. member did not intend to suggest it, but there seems to me to be a flaw in the bill in that respect. If any one has moved from his home town and taken up residence permanently in some other place it is not fair that he should be able to vote with the congregation in the church from which he has removed. That, however, appears to be in the bill and perhaps we shall have to take it unless we are prepared to amend the present provision. The amendment I propose would meet the difficulty of railwaymen or fishermen who might happen to be out of town on the night the meeting was being held. Then, take the case of parents with young children, either the mother or the father would have to stay home, and this would create a great hardship on many people interested in their church. It seems to me, in view of the fact that the two previous votes were taken by ballot, that this vote should be taken in the same manner.

I would suggest that this
amendment is out of order; we have had no notice of it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That question arose in my mind a few minutes ago, but rule 112 applies only to "important" amendments, amendments which are very material to the principle involved, such as were submitted yesterday. But this amendment, it strikes me, is of minor importance. The manner of taking a vote does not affect the principle of the bill at all, and therefore I do not think that this is an important amendment within the meaning of the rule. The amendment before the committee deals purely with the question of procedure.

Of course, if the hon. member
objects I will ask you, Mr. Chairman, to let the section stand, but I would rather see the bill go through quickly.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I rule that this amendment does not require notice.

Who are to have the
privilege of voting-members of the congregation or members of the church?

It is set out in clause (b).
I do not think it is necessary to read it. It seems to me that to accept the amendment that has been proposed would open up a good deal of confusion in taking the vote. All parties concerned have the same chance to vote and I think anyone who is sufficiently interested will be at the meeting where the vote is taken. I cannot agree to this amendment, Mr. Chairman, and I would ask that the section be passed as it stands.

Mr. Chairman, this
matter was very fully discussed from all angles in the Private Bills committee. The method of voting was not challenged. As chairman of that committee I strongly support the bill as it stands.

I think the request of
the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) is a most reasonable one. I was not in attendance in the committee, but it would strike the ordinary man that the proper way to vote under circumstances of this kind would be by ballot. In almost every society and every incorporated company absentees are permitted to vote by proxy, and certainly the whole membership of the church should be entitled to oast a vote on such an important question as that involved. What injury is going to be done the promoters of the bill if this privilege is accorded? What difficulty is going to arise? The privilege will apply to both sides, those for and those against. It is the course adopted by the church authorities on two former occasions, why not follow it on this occasion? I think the hon. member for Brandon is taking rather an odd course in opposing what would appear to an ordinary member of this House to be a most reasonable proposal.

May I point out
that the votes taken in 1911 and 1915 were not decisive votes, but were intended to be merely a guide for the courts. This particular vote will be decisive.

Is not that all the more
reason why everybody should have a chance to vote?

Of course they will have a chance to vote. If we are going to have a real test of the wishes of the congregation, we must have something more systematic than the rather loose method of distributing ballots to the congregation to be signed at pleasure, I quite agree with the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. McGiverin) that the discussion in the Private Bills committee was quite full. The reason for leaving the section in its present form was that it comes nearest to what is the practice in the church now. In my experience I have never 'mown any important question determined by oallot, it has always been by a vote of the nembers of the congregation present.

I am going to put a case to my hon. friend, and I think it is typical of what might happen in many other families. There are five votes in my family. If this meeting is called some time in the autumn or during the winter, four of these votes will in
United, Church of Canada

ill human possibility be scattered in. various parts of Ontario. Is it incumbent upon me to pay the expense of bringing my family to the meeting to vote? I think the case has only to be stated to be refuted. Voting by ballot is the rule in universities, in churches, in joint stock banks, and the like. What objection is there to the proposal? If there is a valid objection we will consider it, but let us hear what the objection is.

I am sure my worthy leader
(Mr. Forke) knows as well as I do that in our western country where the villages and towns are small-and I call this to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) -the majority of the congregations are composed of people living in the surrounding country. Just picture, in our western plains, a meeting being called and only 40 or 50 per cent of the people having an opportunity to attend it owing to a storm. That very serious handicap would be obviated by the method suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Duff). If I have a complaint to make it is that the whole attitude in this matter is based altogether upon an urban point of view; I want the committee to be broad and to have some regard for the interests of the people in the country who would find it impossible to attend this meeting called at a specific time for a specific purpose.

Having been a supporter of
church union-indeed, in the congregation where I worship we have had church union in practice now for three or four years-it does seem to me that the proposal of the hon. member (Mr. Duff) is most reasonable. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) refers to his own family; there are cases in my family that I know of where the people are unable to attend church, although they are very strongly attached to their church. I venture to say that if the congregation wanted i contribution for missionary work or for the minister they would not hesitate to provide those people with an envelope to be sent in. There is no good reason why this amendment cannot be accepted; it will give people who are unable to attend church an opportunity of voting upon this question.

I think there is very real
objection to the proposal. We shall make a great mistake if we seek to reason from analogies drawn from the practices of other corporations, because they follow the practice prescribed in the rules and regulations under which they are constituted. In my judgment this House should not seek to impose upon the churches any method of taking a vote that 
is not prescribed by their own rules and procedure. The method adopted by all churches in arriving at a decision of such importance as this is just the method that is here indicated. Even if we did not indicate in this bill the method by which the rote shouid be taken, the vote would be taken in such a way as to achieve the best results. I do not think the House should undertake to say to any of the churches: You must take your vote thus and so. It is true we have put this provision in the bill, but that is simply adopting the method that is followed by all churches in coming to important decisions at regularly called church meetings.
The minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has answered the objection that was raised, and I am sure the answer was given more than once in the committee when reference was made to former votes. It is true that votes were taken by the Presbyterian church.

Do they not always vote
for elders in the Presbyterian church by ballot?
Always.
The hon. member (Mr. Brown) is not a Presbyterian; he does not know our rules.

Apart altogether from that, there are very real objections. This is a matter upon which important issues depend, and I can see objections to distributing ballots loosely throughout the country. It is urged that it would be just as fair for one side as the other; well, the same may be said for the other method. In all elections taken for any purpose it is inevitable that some people lose their franchise, and in this case it seems to me that the vote should be taken in harmony with the procedure commonly observed. I know that elders are elected in the way that has been indicated, but is that true when it comes to the disposition of property? I rather think not. And, remember that great property interests are involved in this matter; large interests are at stake involving not only local congregations but the property of the church generally all over the Dominion. I think it is desirable that we should adopt the system set forth in this clause.

It would be a very bad
thing to allow the impression to go abroad throughout Canada that there is a desire on the part of anybody in this parliament or out of it to limit in any way the vote of the people interested in this movement. In the circumstances related by the hon. member (Mr. Duff), a large proportion of the membership could not possibly attend the meeting. We

United Church of Canada
know from common experience in regard to voting at elections that in most cases the husband and wife cannot go together: the woman cannot be taken from the home where there are infant children unless some grown person can be left with them. We know that from every family there are absentees who cannot get a chance to vote. A large number of our population constitute a travelling population. These people are usually at home on the Lord's day, but may be miles away during the week when this meeting is called. Is there to be a deliberate attempt to deprive that large and interested population of * vote in regard to what is to them perhaps one of the most sacred things in life? When we ask for objections to my hon. friend's proposal, all we_ get is the suggestion that loose methods may be employed in regard to these ballots. Surely not, in the hands of church dignitaries. Surely we can trust somebody in the churches to see that everybody gets a fair, full and free vote. Why oppose it? What have we to fear from it? The object of everybody should be to get as large and influential a vote as possible on these questions. Do not try to hamper it; do not try to limit it. Get the inclusive idea into your head, not the exclusive idea. See that everybody who has a vote is given every facility to register that vote, and that no obstacle is placed in his way.

I am not going to differ
from the excellent opinions expressed by my hon. friend, but so far as I can judge, this amendment, which is vital in its character, means something more than merely providing for a vote by ballot.

I am not a lawyer, and of
course I do not know as to that. This was cne of the amendments submitted in the committee, and it is quite possible that it may go a little further than it should. But :f the amendment does go further; if it interferes with anything else, I am quite willing to have that additional thing struck out. All I want is that the vote be taken by ballot instead of at a congregational meeting. I am not trying to put anything over on the committee at all.

I am not suggesting that.
But the amendment does appear to me to go much further than simply to provide that the vote shall be by ballot. First the amendment says:
In accordance with regulations set out in schedule D of this act,-
The schedule was attached to the amendment. If my hon. friend will permit me, I would like to read that schedule, because it would be part of the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
A schedule cannot be
put into this part of the bill.
It can be put in somewhere.

I think the committee
is very much confused. There is no such schedule in the bill. Schedule "C" is the last section we have in the bill as it is now before the committee.

I might explain that I attached it when I sent it up, but it was sent back to me. I wanted to read it and explain that this vote is not -going to be a loose vote as the Minister of Agriculture said it was going to be.

What I am coming to is
this:	In considering this amendment, with
the proposed schedule attached thereto, we are considering a vital amendment to the bill. Whether it is good or bad, I am not going to express an opinion for the moment, but we are considering what is undoubtedly a vital amendment to the bill, and I -think we ought to be very careful-not with the idea that the hon. member is attempting to put anything over at all-to see that we do not interject into the bill an amendment which will vitally affect what is the intention of the bill at the present time. Let me read the amendment:
That section 10 be amended as follows:
I pause &,t t'hiait point ito say that one would gather from tlhe reading that 'that meant a substitution, but when I go -a step further I gather that the intention is to add to the clause. Am I correclt in that?
Yes.

Then the intention is
to add to subclause (a) of section 10 the following:
Provided always that if any congregation in connection or in communion with any of the negotiating churches shall upon a vote of such congregation to be taken by ballot in accordance with the regulations set out in schedule "D" of this act-
Which schedule, I understand now, is to be added.
-decide by a majority of the votes cast not to enter the United church, then and in such case the property real and personal belonging to or held in trust for or to the use of such congregation shall remain unaffected by this act and provided that any church formed by the non-concurring congregations shall stand in the place of the respective negatiating church in respect of any trust related to such property. Any

United Church of Canada

vote of such congregation taken in accordance with the provisions of any act of any province of Canada respecting the United church passed before the passing of this act shall be deemed a valid vote for the purpose of this section.
What I want to point out is that the nature of this amendment is so far-reaching that before I would even attempt to pass approval or disapproval I would like to know whether the counsel pro and con in this case have given iit consideration, and whether those who are promoting the bill and those vho are resisting it have been fully consulted ind are conversant with the nature of the amendment.
There was no clause discussed more fully in committee than this particular one.

And the amendment was
rejected by the committee?
And rejected by the committee.
It was not rejected.

I want to make my point clear. I am not in a position to offer any criticism of this amendment without a good deal of study, but I would hesitate to give immediate approval offhand to its inclusion in the bill.

As a member of the
committee in which this clause was discussed, I might say that the petitioners are not opposed to a ballot. The ballot might be taken at this meeting
4 p.m. or the people might declare their wish by open vote. But, as I understand it, in six of the provinces legislation has already been passed prescribing a certain method of voting, and the clause in the bill is in harmony with that method. To alter it, I think, would only cause confusion. I might add that it is a provincial matter.

My hon. friend means
that the clause as it now stands is in harmony with the provincial law?

Yes, the clause as it
now stands.

Perhaps we could defer consideration of this clause and see if we could not get together on it. It seems to me most unreasonable to take away the right of ballot from these people. We have been extending the franchise in this House; it is a principle we have ourselves adopted. We allow certain classes to vote two or three days before election day. Perhaps my hon. friend 
from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) would be willing to compromise and let the congregations decide whether they wanted to vote in congregation meeting; have it optional; give them local autonomy. I suggest that we might let the clause stand and perhaps hon. members might get together upon it.

I think the suggestion a
very good one.

Voting for elders by ballot
has been mentioned. The ballot has always got to be held at a church meeting, the ballots are never sent out.

At my church they are
out on the collection plate.

My hon. friend from Brandon
is mistaken. The ballots are taken out by members of the congregation to people who do not come to church, and they send their ballots in by their friends, who put them on the collection plate.
I happen to be an elder myself.

I cannot help that. You do
not follow the rules of the church in your congregation.

Does that hold good in
the other two churches, Methodist and Congregational?
I do not know.

It appears to me that the
hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Brethen) has mentioned a point that is of very great importance, and that is that legislation has been passed in six provinces providing for a method of voting. If this amendment of the hon. member for Lunenburg were adopted, it might cause two votes to be taken in several congregations in these provinces where legislation has already been passed. To my mind, it is of vital importance that this clause stand as it is, on account of the conflict the amendment might bring about. In regard to voting by ballot, I see no reason why a congregational meeting could not be called for a full day.

How would the people who
are sick in bed or out of town get to that meeting?
How do they get to a government election now?

We are not talking about
that.

United, Church of Canada

They would be in exactly
the same position as if it were a Dominion or provincial election. Persons who wished to vote and were in a position to vote could vote if you had a congregational meeting for the full day. In view of the provincial legislation, I think it is absolutely essential that this clause should stand as it is.

Would the hon. member for
Lunenburg allow me a question? In view of the provincial legislation that has been passed, does not this relate wholly to property in the Territories?
What do you mean by Territories?
I mean outside the provinces.
Oh no. It is the congregational property.

Great stress was laid
by counsel for the promoters on the provincial legislation that had already been passed, and that this clause was an exact reproduction of the clause that had gone into the provincial legislation, and that to have two methods of voting would cause confusion. There was a long discussion in the committee, and a vote was not challenged. Having decided in that way in regard to the voting, and particularly in view of the provincial legislation that has been passed, and as my hon. friend from East Peterborough has just stated as civil rights and property are concerned, it seems to me it would be wiser to adopt the clause as it stands.

Does the chairman of
the committee contend that because this clause was not particularly challenged in the way of a vote in the committee, we are estopped or debarred from asking this House to amend the clause?

Not at all, but I say
the question was threshed out in the committee.

Yes, but it was never
satisfactory to those who were objecting to it, at any point. I might point out that another matter was decided in the committee and decided by vote, and yet this House changed it.

I am not saying for
a moment that this House has not the right to amend the clause. I am simply as chairman supporting the action of the committee on this clause, as I did on the other clause. That does not mean that the House will follow my advice, as was seen last night.
238i

As one who did
not take part in the discussion yesterday or previously, and as one who has no serious objection to union, provided the rights and privileges of the minority are protected, and following the promise of many members who spoke last night that a fair deal would be given, I think the proposition by the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) is only right and fair. At the time of the last vote I was in France and had not the privilege of voting, and when I returned home I found my church voted away from me. Furthermore, this would be about the only case in which the members of the Presbyterian church, especially the nonconcurring members would have the right to vote. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) said that the last vote of 1915 was only a slip vote and nobody paid much attention to it. If we are desirous now of having the matter go through with some kind of harmony, I think it would be in the interests of those promoting the bill to see that a fair opportunity be given to people to express their views. I would like to call attention to the fact that the lay people of the Presbyterian church-and this vote will probably refer to them-had not as a body the privilege of voting. The voting element lies in the kirk session of the congregation to begin with-the ministers and the elders. Next it is in the presbytery-still the ministers and the elders; in the synod it is the minister and the elders, and in the General Assembly it is the ministers and1 the elders. By the Barrier Act the vote of the General Assembly is referred back to the presbytery. It is only referred back to the people who voted on it previously. I should like to see this matter settled with' unanimity and harmony, and I do not think that, as far as the Presbyterian church is concerned, anything except a ballot would be accepted by them. That is the commonest method we have in the church of voting at the present time. The tendency of the time is to extend the ballot to as many people as possible. The taking of a vote at a church meeting would, in my opinion, be a haphazard method, and if a mistake were made they could not rectify it. It is important at this time to have harmony, and if possible to repair a slip which is a very serious matter for the community at large. It is not so much a general thing as it is a congregational matter. I say that vote should be made as large as possible, and I know of no other way that will satisfy the congregation, who will likely be the non-concurring ones, as the ballot, and I would appeal to those who stated that they were willing to give the minority the best possible deal. I think a vote would go a

United Church of Canada
long way to satisfy many who are dissatisfied at the present time.

As far as congregational property and the disposal of that property are concerned, the question must be determined by provincial legislation. I may be stupid but I cannot see how this provision affects it at all.

The ballot is the
system we are all contending for politically and in every other way, and it is the system in the Presbyterian church at the present time.

That must be determined by
provincial legislation.

I think another matter which is lost sight of is the provision in the first part of subsection (b) which says that only those persons who are in full membership and whose names are on the roll of the church at the time of the passing of the act can vote. There is no possibility of stuffing the ballot box under that section. The ballots will be checked up by the church roll. I do not see that any objection can be taken to the proposal. This does not interfere with provincial rights, because it is a provision that will govern the administration of the act when it comes into force.

I quite agree with the
hon. member, but the legislature of Nova Scotia passed a bill this year which was practically the same as this measure, but they provided that not only communicants but adherents should have the right to vote.
Is the hon. gentleman speaking as a lawyer?
Yes.
Or as a member of parliament?

I am speaking as a member of this House who happens to belong to the legal profession. I have no quarrel with the hon. gentleman's proposition to decide the dogmas of your respective churches, and I have felt during the whole course of this debate that hon. members were getting far away from the points . which should be discussed.
Is this section (b) the hon. member refers to?

No. I was coming to the
point when the hon. gentleman interrupted, that under the provisions of the Nova Scotia act adherents have the right to vote. Under this act as we are passing it only communicants have the right to vote.
[Mr. A. E. Ross.l
The section says that where-ever it has been passed by the provincial legislature a different form of voting takes place.

Is the hon. gentleman

Any real or personal property belonging to or held by or in trust for or to the use of any congregation, whether a congregation of the negotiating churches or a congregation received into the United church after the coming into force of this act solely for its own benefit, and in which the denomination to which such congregation belongs has no right or interest, reversionary

-and any appointment so made by him or to fill any vacancy among the members of the commission, or any order of the chief justice on the application of any interested party confirming the appointment of the commission, shall be final and conclusive and shall not be subject to review by any court. Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Bills of Exchange Act

Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Bills of Exchange Act, Revised Statutes, 1906, Chapter 119, by providing a tariff of fees to be charged by notaries for their services in all the provinces for presenting and noting for non-acceptance or non-payment any bill of exchange or promissory note, for protesting the 6ame, keeping the same on record, furnishing copies and sending notices, and other matters incidental thereto.
Will the minister explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Section 124 of the Bills of Exchange Act provides that notaries in each province may charge the fees heretofore allowed them. In the eastern provinces those fees were fixed before confederation. In the West the fees have been regulated by usage. The result is that there is lack of uniformity in the fees charged by notaries for protesting bills of exchange, the scale being different in each province. For instance, in Ontario the fee for protest is 50 cents, for each notice 25 cents; Quebec, $1 and 50 cents; Nova Scotia, 50 cents and 25 cents; New Brunswick, $3. covering protest and all notices; Prince Edward Island, 50 cents and 25 cents, and for outside bills a lump charge of $2.50; Manitoba, $1 and 50, cents; Alberta, Saskatchewan, Yukon and the Northwest Territories, $2 and 50 cents; British Columbia, a lump charge of $2.50. The amendment proposed is for the purpose of having a uniform tariff for all the provinces, and jthe basis which has been adopted is that prevailing in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Yukon and the Northwest Territories, namely, $2 for protest and 50 cents for each notice. This amendment has been requested by the bar of Ontario and by the Chamber of Notaries of the province of Quebec. The bill has been submitted to the governing body of these professions and has been accepted by them.

I am in entire concurrence with the idea of uniformity. I wonder however if it is such an integral part of the law relating to bills of exchange that it is within the constitutional power of this parliament. A notary is of course a provincial officer; he receives his commission from the province and his duties may be defined by the province. I think a provincial officer has a right to fix the fees. I wish I felt otherwise, because I think the proposition is a beneficial one. Has the minister given consideration to the constitutional standpoint?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. I know in the
province of my hon. friend a statute has been passed fixing the fees.
That was done some years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes; and Maclaren on
Bills, Notes and Cheques says regarding the New Brunswick statute:
As the parliament of Canada has exclusive jurisdiction over bills of exchange and promissory notes, the constitutionality of this provincial act is open to question. It is said that the charge still usually made in this province is that in force before the act in question.
So I really think there is no doubt that this parliament has full jurisdiction in every matter relating to bills of exchange.

I do not want to protest,
because in one sense I agree with this legislation. I think there is quite a distinction that we undoubtedly can make, and that is that a protest shall occur in a certain event, and the fixing of remuneration for a provincial officer performing a service by virtue of his provincial commission. I am not making an objection, but let us hope that the differences are not so great that any one will be compelled to raise the question before the courts.

It seems to me the
minister should take into consideration that the business people of the country are being taxed pretty well now and the fees are large enough at the present time.

I should like to endorse
that statement. Has the minister had any application from Manitoba to increase the fees in that province? I understand the fee is only about half the amount fixed in the bill. Is the minister going to increase the fees in Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not heard from
Manitoba, but the fees which will be adopted are those prevailing in Saskatchewan and Alberta.
But not in Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

I have no objection to the
resolution, but I warn the minister that when we go into committee I shall object to the scale of fees he proposes.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee on the resolution, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

The Bar association
appears to have petitions for a uniform schedule, and the schedule provided in the resolution appears to be the highest in force anywhere. I must say I do not believe I would have yielded to that if I had been the minister. It seems to me the lawyers have never needed any help to raise their fees.

Inland Water Freight Rates

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In this instance they
cannot do it without this legislation.

If a Manitoba notary is
charging one dollar for a protest, does the minister say he cannot charge two dollars, unless we pass this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. In Manitoba the
fees are regulated by usage only. In Quebec and Ontario they come under a subsection of section 124; they must charge the fees which were heretofore allowed them. These fees existed before confederation. The fee of fifty cents for a protest, which is charged in Ontario, is not a proper fee when compared with two dollars which is charged in my right hon. friend's province.

This is not a case of
reduction of tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
It is a case of jacking the fees up pretty well.

Why does the minister
not make it one dollar?

Does the minister think it
is right to raise the fee in Manitoba by law? -to double the amount which is now charged simply as a matter of usage? Is that not what he proposes to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I really believe it is a
good thing to have a uniform fee for notarial protests on bills of exchange in all Canada.

As I understand the minister, the rate now in force in Canada varies from fifty cents up to two dollars. I have no objection to the minister making the rate uniform, but I object to placing the rate at the highest figure which now obtains in Canada. I think the fee of two dollars which is charged in Alberta is unreasonable, considering the amount of work connected with a protest. The notary simply takes a printed form, which probably costs one cent, inserts a few figures and words in it, puts his seal on it, hands it out and charges two dollars. I think the service is not rendered commensurate with the fee, and I would suggest to the minister that before the bill is brought down he should give careful thought to the matter of fees charged, and place them at not more than one dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is making sure I will not prolong the session on
account of this bill. I have had requests from the Bar of Ontario, from the Chamber of Notaries of Quebec and others for this legislation.
Does the bill fix two dollars and fifty cents?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Or is that the maximum?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, that is the fee fixed. In all the provinces the notaries may charge a fee for their services in accordance with the tariff provided, I am almost sure they will charge that fee.

I understand in Ontario the
fee is fifty cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Does the minister not think Ontario would be well satisfied with an Increase of a hundred' per cent? Then the minister could bring the other provinces down to the level.
Say one dollar.

One dollar, and we will make
it unanimous.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would suggest that
the resolution be carried and the bill be introduced, and when it comes back to committee the objection might be raised then. Perhaps it will not be objected to.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Lapointe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 212, to amend the Bills of Exchange Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. T. A. LOW (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Inland Water Freight Rates Act, 1923, and to provide,-
1.	That it be enacted in lieu of the provisions of section three thereof as to filing with the Board of Grain Commissioners of a tariff of rates to be charged, that every shipper (including a corporation) shall immediately after entering into any charter party, bill of lading or contract for the carriage of grain from Fort William or Port Arthur to any other port or place in Canada or the United States by lake or river navigation, and before the grain shall have been laden in pursuance thereof, file with the Board of Grain Commissioners of Canada a true copy of the said charter party, bill of lading or contract for carriage.
2.	That the provisions as to posting up statements in detail of cargo space, time of shipment and destination, as prescribed by section six, be repealed, and that the penalty clauses of the said act be amended.
Inland Water Freight Rates
Explain.

When this act was passed
last session, it was passed with one object in mind, and that was to secure information regarding tariff rates and charges between Fort William and Bay, and American ports. As frequently follows in implementing new legislation we found some difficulty during the fall, and that was when the question arose as to whether the American vessel owners would comply with the provisions of the act. They hesitated for some time, but ultimately came in. The object of the amendment is to enable us to secure the information from the source from which it is possibly most easily secured, that is from the shippers, who will be compelled under this amendment to file with the Canada Grain Board a copy of their tariffs-

Shippers have
not a tariff.

They have a copy of the
contract made with the ship owners.
That is a charter party; that is not a tariff.

It is a tariff so far as they
are concerned. The information would be obtained perhaps a little more easily in that way than through the American ship owners.

Is my hon.
friend quite sure that he is giving the real object for passing the legislation last year? The object, we were told, as I recollect it, was that we were going to regulate these rates on the lakes, not merely get information regarding them.

The object last year was to
secure, so that the public would be able to secure it, the information. It proved perhaps a little difficult to secure it through the American vessel owners, and we are therefore amending the act that we may secure it from the source from which it is perhaps most easily secured, and that is from the shipper. When the bill comes down the object of the amendment will be fully explained to the House.

Is it the pleasure of the
House to adopt the motion?

I think we had better call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

The motion was made
by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) that the House go into committee to consider the resolution in reference to Inland Water Freight Rates. I understood the hon. member for West York (S5r Henry Drayton) desired to speak to the question, but he is not present.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee on the resolution, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
I am not quite clear as to why there should be any amendment to the bill to accomplish the purpose. Has the bill not been interpreted to mean this already?

It has been so interpreted by
the chairman of the Canada Grain Board, but some legal gentlemen have raised a question, on the interpretation and we thought it well to have the matter settled.
What legal gentlemen?

Legal gentlemen connected with the Grain Exchange in Winnipeg. The idea is simply, as I stated earlier in the day, to provide a means to obtain necessary information, as I stated, also the American vessel owners hesitated for some time about coming in this autumn but ultimately came in. The object of the proposed amendment is to provide that the shipper will be compelled to file a copy of the contract or charter. The words are very simple. The vessel-owner will not be called upon to file a tariff.
Do I understand the minister to say that the American vessel owner on the Great Lakes will not be compelled to file his tariff?

He will not be compelled to file his tariff, nor will any other vessel owner; but the shipper will be compelled to file the
contract.
It is really an abandonment of the idea in last year's legislation to fix and control rates.
Yes, so far as the vessel owners are concerned.
It is an abandonment of the idea of controlling rates on the Great Lakes?

No, not at all. The main
object last year was to secure information in regard to the rates which they were charging and the space they were selling.

Inland Water Freight Rates

The minister said that
was the main object. What good was that information going to be? How would it be used? Information is not a thing in itself; it is a means to an end. What was the information for?

In order that the public might
know the rates that were being charged, and that the Canada Grain Board might have this information.
The minister's answer to the question is that the information was wanted so that the public might have it and the Canada Grain Board might also have it.
Yes.

What good was it to be
either to the public or the Canada Grain Board?

I do not think anybody will
deny that it will be some benefit to the people of the country, particularly the grain growers, to know the rates that are being charged and the space that is being let from time to time.
This information is of no use to them unless it serves some purpose. What is to be done with it?

Information as to the price actually paid for some commodity sold throughout the country is of decided advantage. As regards the grain trade to-day, information concerning the iprice of wheat can be received by telegraphic communication.

I am free to admit that
the people ought to know what is being paid, but they want to know it for a purpose. What good does it do to the western farmer to know that he is paying, say six cents a bushel for "wheat shipped on the lakes unless he can make some use of the information?

Does my right hon. friend
attempt to argue for one moment that it is of no interest to the farmers of tlhe West to know the rate or the price of "wheat that prevails from day to day?

I never argued that.
It is of great interest to them to know that, but I would not think it would be worth while putting a statute through just so that they should have that information. I do not think the fanners have had very much difficulty in obtaining 'that information all along. The farmers know that they are being charged this rate, and I 'have never heard the farmers complain of lack of information. What they are complaining about is that they are being 239
charged this rate. They thought the act of last session was for the purpose of enabling a government body to reduce the rate. Of course the minister contended that the old act was to regulate the rates, but he says now that it is just for the purpose of getting the information as to the rates. It is quite evident that he had abandoned all idea, if it ever did exist, of regulating the rates, because I do noit know how he could regulate rates with the interpretation of last October and with this new act which makes the interpretation law.

Does my right hon. friend
not know that the Canada Grain Board can say to the shipper that the rate is too high? If the rate reaches a point which they consider too high, they can intervene and fix the rate.

I admit that the board
can say to the shipper that the rate is too high. This reminds me of the Shakespearian phrase:
Why, so can I, or so can any man;
But will they come when you do call for them?
When they do say that the rate is too high, does that make it any lower?
Where does that quotation come from in Shakespeare? Can he quote it all?

I cannot compete with
the hon. member on some things, but I am inclined to think that on that subject I can.
I can call spirits from the vasty deep.
Why, eo can I, or so can any man;
But will they come when you do call for them?
Where does the hon. member think it is
from?
Owen Glendower.

I fear he is wrong. I
si ould like him to look it up. Now, if we will come from Shakespeare to the bill-
Shakespeare's name was Bill.

So is that of the hon.
member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff). How is the board going to fix the rate after the rate is fixed? What I mean is this:	When
the charter party is made, everything is completed, and the board is told that it is completed at a certain rate. What can the board do then?

Should the rate have reached
a point which the board thinks too high, it can step in and fix the rate. Is there anything in this legislation that the right hon. member would like me to drop? If there is, I would be glad to hear it. I do not think



Inland Water Freight Rates
the right hon. gentleman opposed the old act of last year very strongly. Does he take objection to anything that I did in connection with that act last fall? One thing, at least, was accomplished, and that is that the rates of last year were lower than the rates of 1922. The act had at least that effect upon the rates. I should like to quote a few words from the Free Press of Winnipeg, of January 10, 1924. Speaking of the investigation that had taken place, this paper says:
As a result of the investigation the Dominion parliament passed the Inland Water Freight Rates Act of 1923 which requires vessel owners to file tariffs of the rates charged for the shipment of grain from Fort William and Port Arthur and gives the Board of Grain Commissioners power to fix maximum rates. This legislation, faithfully prepared, has been found in some details defective. But its effects on the whole have been beneficial, and in spite of a temporary difficulty owing to American vessel owners objecting to file their rates, a much larger tonnage of grain was moved on the lakes in the fall of 1923 than in the previous year, and at a substantially lower rate.

I would just
refer the minister to the Free Press on the cne hand to himself on the other and what he said only a few weeks ago on this very question of rates, when he admitted that there was a very substantial increase in rates in September, when he again admitted that there was a substantial increase in rates in October. There is no doubt about the truth of this thing.

You cannot pick out one
thing. The average is the only thing that counts.

Supposing we
ge't down to facts. What I said and what he agreed to was that ordinarily the rates from Fort William to Buffalo and from Duluth to Buffalo were the same.
The minister agrees. I showed that owing to this hastily rushed through and improvident legislation, American boats would not participate in that business. That was not business of a kind that was at all affected by coastal business one way or the other. It was a movement from a Canadian port to an American port, and American boats alwaj^s took part in that movement. They stopped for the simple reason that they would not submit themselves to Canadian jurisdiction as was contemplated by the legislation. While under ordinary conditions the rates were always exactly the same, in September last the Duluth-Buffalo rate ranged from 2 1-2 cents to 2 3-4 cents; and) on September 20 the Fort William-Buffalo rate had reached 5 cents. The admission was made the other day that the average of the Canadian rates for that

month was, from Fort William to Buffalo, 4.9 as I recollect it, and I am sure that is correct. The minister's admission was 4.5 as against 2 1-2 and 2 3-4 from Duluth. These were admitted facts. Then in October the Fort William-Buffalo rate reached its peak of 6 1-2 cents, while the Duluth-Buffalo rate was 3 cents. And that again is admitted. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) was here the other day and said he saw no sense in the minister's making out that the rates were low at that time when every one knew they were high. And why were they high? They were high simply because the American boats which had always been in the business and held down the Fort William rate to a parity with the Duluth rate would not enter our ports as a result of this legislation. What was done then? The result obtained last year was altogether in spite of this legislation, that is all. Under this legislation the American carrier had to file his tariffs and submit himself to the jurisdiction of the board so that the board could reduce his rates if they were too high. By filing his tariffs he would place himself in that position, and he would not do so. How was the difficulty overcome? Was it overcome by means of this bill? No; the thing was adjusted in spite of this half-baked and hasty legislation. Why, we had the nonsensical ruling which said that in addition to the carrier filing his charter party and tariff, a further burden was to be placed on the trade:	the shippers were to be put
in the position of defending the carriers' rates. We usually think there is an issue between the carrier and the shipper; here under this nonsensical ruling, which I admit had to be done under the circumstances as a result of this legislation- which was largely ludicrous-

Why does my hon. friend not
quote some Canadian rates from Fort William to bay ports? If he does he will find they were lower than in the previous year.

The minister
knows very well that he could not affect these rates one way or the other by the ball; not one order was made, not a single thing was done. As early as July 7 in that year Mr. James Stewart wired to the then Minister of Trade and Commerce asking that the coastal shipping laws should be suspended because he was being charged a higher rate from Fort William to Port Colbome than Canadian vessel owners were charging from Fort William to Buffalo. Mr. Stewart kept on sending 240i
wires occasionally to the department. I notice on August 29, he sent the following wire:
J. A. Robb,
Minister of Trade and Commerce,
Ottawa.
Buffalo now two cents Port Colborne still three and three-quarters. We respectfully ask for suspension coasting laws immediately as American tonnage offered for Port Collborne at two cents. Kindly confirm so as enable Canadian milis compete with Buffalo mills.
A little later on, on September 8, Le wired again:
Have had no reply respecting permission load American bottoms for Port Col'bome. Combine has already cost us about fifty thousand dollars and respectfully poinit out we now consider ourseUves free use any reasonable method expose and rectify situation.
I do not wish to take up the time of the committee in reading many of these communications, but I have quite a number of them from grain shippers applying to the government for a suspension of these laws. I should like to bring to the attention of the committee a statement made by the Secretary of the Dominion Millers' Association, Mr. C. B. Watts, who, I presume, would be an unprejudiced man in regard to this matter. This is a letter to the Hon. Charles Stewart, Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa, it is dated November 4, 1922:
Possibly you are not aware that as high as eleven cents per bushel is being paid to take wheat from Fort William to bay ports or Goderich a government boat, Pathfinder, having been relet by James Richardson and Sons at this figure, due to load in a few days.
The normal freight this time of the year would be four cents, but the general bid rate now is 8 cents.
Further on in his letter he says:
The extra freight, be it 4 cents, 6 cents, or 7 cents per bushel is that much money taken out of the pockets of the western farmers, or equivalent to over $400,000 to possibly $600,000 or $700,000 on shipments the last week in October alone of 10,910,000 bushels.
Further on he says:
The rail freight from the lake ports to Montreal is only 8% cents per bushel, no less than 17 cents per bushel I know and it is reported that 18.J cents per bushel, has been paid from Buffalo to Montreal by water.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has just told us that the rates last year in August were one fifth of a cent higher than in 1922, in September, one half of a cent higher, in October, two fifths higher. But in the year 1922 in these very months the government were receiving wires from shippers at Fort William asking for the suspension of the coastal laws. The government apparently thought that they had not the power to suspend the coastal laws in 1922 and they came to parliament last year and got legislation to enable them to do so. But although the rates

were higher in 1923 in these three months than they were in 1922, the government so far as I know did not suspend the coastal laws. These shipping laws are kept on the statute books for the purpose of building up a merchant marine in Canada and I want to quote one paragraph from a letter from the secretary of the Marine and Shippers Association to the minister:
The coasting law is the only solid foundation on which the shipbuilding industry of Canada rests. Destroy confidence in it and you prevent investments in Canadian ships. Without a rigid coasting law to parallel that of the United States Canadian tonnage would have to take the only means open to it to enjoy equal rights with that of the United States and no more building would take place in Canada.
James Whelan, president of the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company, in a letter to the government at the time when there was some talk of suspending the coastal shipping laws
says:
Looking to the future we are justified in anticipating a large expansion in the Canadian West with future crops constantly increasing far beyond the amount of the present bumper one.
Although they had a bumper crop to handle in 1922 the Canadian producer was being robbed as was pointed out in Mr. Watt's letter to the government. The government sat here apparently thinking they had no power to act although I find in some correspondence I have here that in November they did allow the American boats to load wheat and bring it down the lakes on their last trip. I urge the minister to remove the coastal shipping law from the statute books because it has been abused shamefully by the ship owners. It has been retained in the belief that it would build up a Canadian shipbuilding industry, and the owners of Canadian shipping and those engaged in the industry have used their power to bleed the Canadian producer. I do not think that term is at all too strong, and if this coastal shipping law has been abused in that way the proper thing is to abolish it. According to a pamphlet issued by the Toronto Board of Trade about 50 per cent of the money invested: in the Canadian shipping industry is American capital. So that apparently we are bleeding ourselves for the benefit of these American millionaires. The farmers are getting tired of this sort of thing and it is not to be wondered at. If the government had done their duty in 1922 and promptly suspended the coastal shipping law when asked to do so by Mr. Stewart possibly there would not now be so much agitation for the abrogation of that law and there would not be all this discussion to-night. The suspension of that law in .the summer of 1922
[Mr. Coote.l
would have brought the Canadian ship owners to their senses and taught them that there is some authority in Canada over them.
I think the minister deserves some credit for the action he took last fall when he found that the legislation which had been enacted was not effective. Either he, or the Board of Grain Commissioners is to be commended, whoever it may be that took the action, in endeavouring to circumvent that legislation. I think the first mistake last year on the part of the government was the failure to promptly suspend the coastal' shipping law. But when it was attempted to regulate this shipping combine by making the shippers file their tariffs the government should have confined that legislation to Canadian vessels. Had that been done they would not have got into the trouble in which they found themselves, as I understand that the American owners of vessels would have come in and carried grain to Buffalo if they had not been asked to file their tariffs.

Would not that have been a
discrimination against the Canadian shipowners?

It might possibly be called
a discrimination, but we are suffering from discrimination now on the part of Canadian vessel owners, because Canadian vessel owners carried grain in 1922 from Fort William to American ports at a cheaper rate than they would carry it to Canadian ports.

The object was to get the
Americans as well as the Canadians to publish their tariffs, and there was nothing wrong in that. It is true that the provision has not worked out as we expected but it was considered at the time advisable. I asked the chairman of the board to put the broadest interpretation he could on the act-
In other words, to say that black was white.

-and to write and let me know what his views were and he told me that it was quite proper under the act to ask the shipper to file the information which we required. It did1 not matter where we got the information if we got it.

That may possibly be all

We are protecting the Canadian ship owner with the coastal law and apparently the government will not be in any hurry to suspend it.

The Americans were required
to give their tariffs as well as the Canadians.

I think there is considerable
force in the argument of some hon. members to my right that the minister is asking the wrong man to file it, and if the penalty clause is invoked and the shipper is fined we shall have a peculiar situation to say the least. It is because of that.. that I suggest to the minister, if he persists in this corrective legislation which is made necessary because of the coastal law, that it is better to compel the ship owner to file the tariff.

Then we are getting only half
the information we require. The Americans will come in and not be subject to the same regulations. Is it right to ask the Canadian vessel owners to do something which we are not asking the foreigner to do?

You are allowing the Canadian ship owner now to do something which you will not allow the foreign shiip owner to do; you are allowing him to carry grain to Canadian ports but not allowing the American ship owners to bring grain to Canadian ports. So that the discrimination against the Canadian ship owner which the minister suggests is more than offset by the privilege which the Canadian ship owners enjoy. If the minister thinks this legislation compelling the filing of rates is necessary, I am not going to labour the point at all.

I will not say offhand that the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) were wrong in the point they raised, but I very reluctantly accept their attitude towards publishing rates on the Great Lakes. Sometimes the farmer is urged to be businesslike, to keep in touch with the world's markets, to know the cost of carrying his grain, so he will know what his grain is worth when he is
selling it. I believe that is sound advice. But how is the farmer to know what his grain is worth if he does not know the cost of carrying it to Liverpool?
The rates will be posted.

Oh no, that is
done away with under this amendment.

That is the very point
which the member for Marquette and the member for Vancouver Centre objected to. I think they argued it would be unfair. Apparently they did not object to the publication of the higher rates,-what they termed the regular rates. That is, it is all right for the farmer to know the higher rates, but if his grain is being carried for two or three cents less he must not know that.

May I make my position clear? I object to the shipper, the individual who buys this space and ships his grain, being compelled to file rates. I do not object to the ship owner or carrier being compelled to do so.
I am very glad the member for Vancouver Centre takes that stand. He has no objection to the farmer knowing from day to day if necessary, the cost of carrying grain across the Great Lakes.
No.

That I believe is advisable. But since it is admitted by the hon. member I will not carry the point any further. Another defect in the proposed bill is this. As we heard, men make a practice of engaging space, not intending to use it themselves, but to resell it at a profit. Now, as I understand this proposed legislation, is it not possible that there will be a missing link, that the carriers might not be charging too much, although the shippers might be paying too much, and the Board of Grain Commissioners, in theory at least, might too hastily penalize the carriers whereas they might not be to blame? Believe American vessel owners will object filing tariffs in accordance with provisions section 3 but see no objection filing copy of charter, personally believe charter should be filed with hopes this will expose and stop speculation on part of vessel brokers who are responsible to neither grain shipper or vessel owner and who have done tremendous harm to vessel interests, some of these vessel brokers not being satisfied with

Unless that is done the pernicious practice which this gentleman complains of will continue and we will not know what the man between is getting, and the minister's object will not be accomplished. I am bound to say that, like my friend from Maoleod (Mr. Coote), I have a little sympathy with the minister in what he tried to do last fall. He had rather a lawless gang to deal with. If they would say to-night that at any time when there is a discrimination of half a cent a bushel- because that is as much discrimination as should 'be allowed between the rates of the Canadian and the American steamships- they will immediately suspend the coastal laws, I think my hon. friends here and our farmers in the west would be satisfied and that the suggestion would act as a very effective club. I have been in the steamboat business now for nearly twenty years, but after listening to what has been said here to-night I am commencing to think that I do not know anything about steamboats. I suggest that the government charter a number of the steamers that they have in the Canadian Government Merchant Marine to these
prairie farmers who are so anxious to get into the steamboat business and give them a chance to demonstrate that they can put them on a paying basis. If they are sincere in what they say and can manage steamboats as well as their remarks would seem to indicate, why should they not take that proposition over? I do not see why we should have ships of the merchant marine which cost this country so many millions of dollars lying idle when there is a body of people so anxious to get into the steamboat business.
A great deal has been said about the coastal laws, and hon. members advocate their suspension. How would that work out? Will the Americans abolish their coastal laws? Not by any means. You cannot run a Canadian steamer from one American port to another American port; at least, you cannot do it on the Pacific coast. If the Canadian coastal laws were suspended, it would mean that the Americans would run their boats between their own ports when they could get a good revenue by so doing, and when work was slack they could switch over and run our Canadian boats out of business. There is no question about it; if the Americans keep their coastal laws in force we have got to keep ours. If some of those men who are talking so much about the steamboat business went into it they would soon get sick of their job. a great deal sicker than they are of raising wheat.
Impossible!

Running a boat on the lakes is entirely different from running a boat on the ocean. You have got to figure your interest, your depreciation, your insurance, with respect to the running of the boats during the open season; the rest of the year they have to be tied up.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Why, certainly.
What experience has he had in running boats on the lakes?

Running steamboats on
the lakes and running them on the coast is the same thing; a steamboat is a steamboat no matter where it is run. I might say not on'ly have I constructed steamers but I have operated them. I do not claim to know all about the business but I do claim to know a little and I can assure you there is not the money in steamboat work that some people think there is; it 'certainly takes a great deal of capital to build boats. The boats that the hon. gentleman saw during the course of his pleasant trip to Kingston and down the river were not serviceable 'boats. I do not think he could get the impression that they were. When this great combine that he speaks about was formed there was more money in the United States than there was in Canada and the best boats in the Canadian service were bought at that time by the American interests-and I am not going to say that some person did not make some profit. Anyway, these 'boats passed into the American service.
The trouble at present in regard to carrying grain is this: We may have sufficient Canadian bottoms to carry what grain may go from Canadian ports to Canadian ports, but those boats could not by any means handle the grain passing from a Canadian port to an American port, therefore we are bound to use the American boats. The act which came into force last year and jto which I referred in my address previously, was an act which was introduced by the present government without any reference to the companies or any person else connected with the service, and the result was that there were bad points in it which could have been avoided had the government taken the proper course. After the act was passed the government went into consultation with the representatives of the steamship companies and told them that the time had now come when they were going to make them "eat crow," and the American steamship owners left them without a service. I am not going to find fault with the government for upset-

ting that law, but I .think they made a mistake in not doing it sooner. If there was not the expected congestion in regard to this transportation of wheat it was because the people did not buy the wheat, being afraid they would not be able to get tihe service. If the government had earlier seen the mistake they made and had attempted to rectify it, I do not think there would have been any increase in rates. Once they realized they had made a mistake after the rate pressure got upon them from Winnipeg, they got the benefit of cheaper rates. I for one would not find fault with breaking the law. They did not do it soon enough in my opinion. I think we should do away with the whole thing now, and I think we would get a better service.

Irrespective of the coasting
law?

Do what you like
about that. That is something you have in your hands and can make use of if necessary, but I do not think the act passed last year or this amendment will be any good.

We had a good deal of discussion in this House the other night in regard to shipping Canadian wheat from Halifax and St. John. Let me now read a letter from one of the biggest grain firms in Canada, which shows that this coastal shipping law is driving our wheat, to the United States, so that it cannot get to Halifax and St. John. It is from James Carruthers and Company, Limited, and is addressed to the Department of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa. It is dated November 30, 1922:

There has been so much delay in getting this matter fixed up-
That is, negotiations had gone on from July to November.
-we don't believe there will be any American boats load cargoes of Manitoba wheat this year for Canadian ports as shippers could not ascertain just what the ruling was and according to the wires we received from Winnipeg there have been no charters made, in fact nearly all the cargoes are going to Buffalo and other American ports.
It is too bad this matter was not settled some time ago as it would have enabled us to bring more wheat to Canadian ports and we would have been able to ship it out during the winter months from St. John and Portland.

That is what goes on every year, because we have not enough Canadian boats to carry our Canadian grain down the lakes. Approximately 50 per cent of it must go to American ports, chiefly Buffalo, and then through American ports on the Atlantic seaboard. First of all, I would like to suggest to the Minister of Railways that he should get into consultation with the hon. member for Cariboo, and possibly he could induce him to manage the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, so that it would show no further losses. It is too late an hour for us to enter into
11 p.m. any discussion of the profits which the ship owners on the Great lakes made in the year 1922, but those profits could, I think, quite properly be called unholy profits. This shipping combine which bled us in 1922, and again I think in 1923, was one of the worst combines that ever existed in Canada, and I do hope that the minister, if he will not suspend the coasting shipping law, will devise some legislation to control this combine, but I repeat, he will not handle it effectively unless he suspends the coasting shipping law.	We have
monkeyed with these shippers long enough. They have had their chances to bleed us and they can now stand a little American competition. At one time it was the proud boast of British sailors that they could compete with the world, but apparently our Canadian sailors are not made of that kind of stuff, and they must have this kind of protection.

word in reply to the ex-Minister of Finance, who has spoken frequently of the shipments to Duluth. During the year 1922-1923 we had the largest quantity of grain in any year since 1917-1918. My hon. friend says the rates were higher because of a lack of boats to dhip the grain, particularly to the port of Duluth, and yet we shipped to Duluth more grain in that year than in any of the previous seven years.
My hon. friend is a little mixed. We do not ship to Duluth, but to Buffalo.
My hon. friend quoted Duluth time and again.

What I was
doing was this, and surely everybody knows it except my hon. friend. The usual rate Fort William-Buffalo corresponds to Duluth-Buffalo; that is the usual thing, but-and I will say this again to my hon. friend, because he has evidently not followed what has been said this evening-by reason of the fact that the American boats could not get into Fort William, their rates, which were practically the same, were almost doubled out of Fort William; that is the Fort William rate was just twice as much as Duluth. speechtext:
I am quite
prepared to strike out the provision as to the right of way to which my hon. friend objects, but it arose- chiefly over the purchase of a right of way for the reservoir line built from the Lake of the Woods to Winnipeg. It crossed a number of school sections and they had a good deal of difficulty. I can quite conceive, however, in connection with a project like that for a railway that, perhaps, it is just as well that the statute does not provide for giving control to the minister, and I am willing to strike that out. If a small site is required for a church, there is, of course, no competition, and the same is the case as regards a school site or a cemetery site. These are the only sites that I am interested in having added to the list that the minister may deal with.

How is the school site
dealt with? By valuation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the same way, but the valuation is made by an officer of the department, which valuation fixes the upset price of the sale. I move to strike out the words " as right of way for any project or "-

I see the note on the
opposite page reads:
There is no way in which strips of land across school lands required as rights of way for drainage, irrigation, pipe line, reservoir or other projects.
Just leaving the other projects out, would it not be as well for the minister to substitute at least a right of way for water supplies or drainage? There would not be much use in building a reservoir if there was not a pipe to draw the water out.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not
anxious to take power to deal with what would involve the crossing of half a dozen sections of land, school lands for example, without consultation, at least, with the provincial authorities or the actual owners of the land.
That is the only objection. For the small parcels, this is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What we
want to deal with is those little acreages of land required for such purposes. The other matter can be one of agreement between the federal government and the provinces.

The only thing I thought
was that the limitation that was suggested was a little too narrow and that it would leave the bill up in the air. If the minister wants this for reservoir purposes, he would get it for reservoir purposes, but he would be deprived of any outlet for his reservoir. He might just as well get a pipe for the reservoir, or not build the reservoir at all.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
On motion of Mr. Graham the House adjourned at 11.25 p.m.
Monday, June 30, 1924
